name: Financial analyst
summary: Financial analyst interviews usually test whether you understand the three financial statements and how they connect, can build or read a model, and can turn numbers into a recommendation. FP&A roles lean towards budgeting, forecasting and explaining variances; equity research and investment roles lean towards valuation and a stock pitch. Many employers add an Excel test or a case for some roles.
rounds: Technical interview on accounting, the financial statements and valuation basics
Excel or modelling test, or a take-home case (for many roles)
Hiring manager interview on past work, a company you follow or, for research roles, a stock pitch
Final round with a senior finance leader or HR
looks_for: How the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement link
Comfort with Excel and building a clean model others can check
Explaining what's behind a number, not just the number
Valuation basics: discounted cash flow, multiples and their limits
Commercial sense: what drives revenue and costs in the business
Accuracy and checking your own work

questions.text: Tell me about an analysis or model you built that someone used to make a decision.
covers: The decision and who was making it
What you built, the key assumptions and how you checked them
What was decided and what happened afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found an error in your own numbers after you'd shared them.
covers: How you found it and how big it was
How quickly you told people and what you corrected
The check you added so it wouldn't happen again

questions.text: Describe a time you explained a financial result to people outside finance.
covers: Who they were and what they needed to decide
How you simplified it without losing accuracy
How you knew they understood, and what they did next

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked to a hard finance deadline, such as a month-end close, a budget or a results date.
covers: What was due, and what made it tight
How you planned, prioritised and checked the work
What you delivered and what you'd do differently

questions.text: Walk me through the three financial statements and how they connect.
covers: What each statement shows, in one line each
How net income flows into the cash flow statement and retained earnings
How the closing cash and debt tie back to the balance sheet

questions.text: Depreciation goes up. Talk me through what changes on each of the three statements.
covers: Lower operating profit and lower tax, so lower net income
Added back on the cash flow statement, so cash ends up higher by the tax saved
Lower asset value on the balance sheet, balanced by more cash and lower retained earnings

questions.text: How would you value a company? Talk me through the main approaches and when you'd use each.
covers: Discounted cash flow: forecast cash flows, discount at the cost of capital (WACC), add a terminal value
Comparable companies and past deals, using multiples such as EV/EBITDA or P/E
Why you'd use more than one method and sense-check the range

questions.text: What's the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
covers: Equity value is what the shares are worth; enterprise value is the whole business, for all its funders
Moving between them: add debt and similar claims, subtract cash
Which multiples go with which, such as EV/EBITDA versus P/E

questions.text: Costs came in well above budget this quarter. How would you explain the variance to leadership?
covers: Splitting the variance into volume, price, mix, one-offs and timing
Which parts the business can control and which it can't
What it means for the forecast and what you'd recommend

questions.text: How would you build a simple revenue forecast for a business like a café chain or an online store?
covers: Breaking revenue into drivers, such as customers, orders per customer and average order value
Where each assumption comes from and how it might change
A base case with upside and downside, rather than one number

questions.text: What's working capital, and why can a growing, profitable company run short of cash?
covers: Current assets minus current liabilities: stock, money owed by customers, bills to pay
Growth ties up cash in stock and unpaid customer invoices before it comes back
Fixes such as faster collection, better supplier terms or less stock

questions.text: Which ratios would you look at to judge whether a company can repay a loan?
covers: Leverage, such as debt to EBITDA, and interest cover
Liquidity and cash: current ratio and cash flow from operations
Trends over several years and what's behind them

questions.text: Pitch me a company you follow. Would you buy, hold or sell its shares, and why?
covers: What the company does and how it makes money, briefly
Two or three reasons for your view, with numbers
The main risk and what would change your mind

questions.text: Which Excel functions and habits do you rely on when you build a model?
covers: Lookups such as XLOOKUP or INDEX-MATCH, SUMIFS and pivot tables
Separate inputs, calculations and outputs, with inputs clearly marked
Checks that totals tie and the balance sheet balances

questions.text: Why finance, and why this side of it: FP&A, research, credit or corporate finance?
covers: What draws you to finance, shown by something you've done
Why this particular kind of role suits you
What you want to learn in it

questions.text: What business or financial news have you followed recently, and what did you make of it?
covers: One specific story, summarised in two sentences
Your own view of what it means for the companies involved
How it connects to the role or the employer's business

questions.text: Are you planning further qualifications, such as the CFA or an MBA, and how do they fit your plans?
covers: An honest answer about your plans
How the qualification would help in this role
How you'd balance study with the job

tips: Practise the three-statement walk-through and the depreciation question out loud until both answers are short and clear.
Know one company well: its business model, recent results, valuation and main risks.
In an Excel test, accuracy beats speed: label inputs, check totals and say what you'd check with more time.
For FP&A roles, prepare a variance story: the drivers you found and what you recommended.
If you've done a finance course or certification, expect to be tested on it, not just asked about it.
End every case with a recommendation, then the risks.
